We believe in the power of teamwork, curiosity, and creative thinking. Every challenge is an opportunity to learn, grow, and turn ideas into reality.

NOVA YEARS — Beyond the Limits of Earth.
summary:
NOVA is an interactive browser-based game that turns space mission design into a hands-on learning experience. Created for the Space Mission Design Game challenge, it addresses a learning gap: mission trade-offs are difficult to understand when engineering choices are taught in isolation.

Players begin with a lunar science goal, then design a mission across six stations: launch, power, instruments, communications, operations, and trajectory. Each choice affects other constraints. An instrument may raise the game’s science score while requiring more mass, power, data, fuel, time, or budget. Players evaluate their design, explore an illustrative mission timeline, and use the debrief to understand the consequences and revise their decisions.

NASA’s LRO lunar model, LROC imagery, and LOLA elevation data ground NOVA’s lunar visualization. NASA mission-design resources inform its learning flow from mission goals through launch, space, ground, and science users. Game values are simplified educational models, not NASA specifications or real-mission predictions.

By making systems thinking visible and interactive, NOVA supports SDG 4 (Quality Education), SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure), and SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production) as learning connections, without claiming measured impact.
details:
Project Details

NOVA is an interactive, browser-based educational simulation game designed for high school students, introductory engineering undergraduates, and space enthusiasts. Bridging the gap between theoretical aerospace concepts and practical mission design, NOVA challenges players to conceptualize, engineer, test, and fly a lunar science mission from initial launch through cislunar transit to final lunar landing. Through real-time 3D environments, interactive controls, and integrated educational guides, learners experience firsthand how every engineering decision ripples across an entire spacecraft system.

The Problem and NOVA's Solution

Designing a real space mission is an exercise in managing conflicting priorities: maximizing scientific return while navigating tightly coupled engineering subsystems and strict physical and financial constraints. In traditional classrooms,disciplines such as propulsion, orbital mechanics, electrical power, payloads, and telecommunications are often taught in separate modules. As a result, students can struggle to see the bigger picture—for example, how choosing a higher-resolution spectrometer does not just increase budget costs, but also adds dry mass, demands larger solar arrays or batteries, generates heavier downlink data volumes, and requires higher-capacity launch services.

NOVA solves this challenge by consolidating these engineering compromises into a unified, hands-on sandbox. Players begin by defining their scientific goals, then configure their spacecraft across six interconnected design stations. Every adjustment triggers immediate recalculations across the entire vehicle, making subsystem dependencies visible in real time. Once the architecture is complete, players launch their mission in a 3D simulation, analyze the post-flight evaluation and diagnostic report to identify bottlenecks or failure points, refine their build, and compare how alternative engineering strategies impact mission success.

Project Links

  • Live Simulation: https://steven556-maker.github.io/nasa-space-mission-game./
  • Source Code (GitHub):  https://github.com/steven556-maker/nasa-space-mission-game..git

Value, Target Audience, and Intended Impact

NOVA serves high school students, introductory engineering undergraduates, and space enthusiasts by transforming abstract aerospace engineering principles into tangible, intuitive experiences. By allowing learners to experiment, fail safely, and iterate without real-world cost or risk, the platform cultivates critical competencies in systems thinking, multi-variable resource allocation, balancing scientific ambition against physical constraints, and data-driven troubleshooting.

The platform aligns its pedagogical framework with three United Nations Sustainable Development Goals:

  • SDG 4 (Quality Education): Expands access to aerospace and systems-engineering education by delivering an interactive, self-paced simulation that requires no specialized lab equipment.
  • SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure): Introduces students to integrated engineering design,subsystem architecture, and quantitative trade-off analysis inspired by real-world aerospace workflows.
  • SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production): Reinforces resource efficiency and optimization under strict mass, energy, and financial budgets.

These connections outline NOVA's intended educational alignment; the project does not claim measured real-world environmental or social impact.

How It Works: The Player's Mission

Players start by selecting one of three core mission profiles—Orbital Survey, Lander, or Surface Science—choosing up to two primary science objectives, and picking a specific lunar target site with distinct lighting, terrain, and communication conditions. From there, they engineer their spacecraft across six Mission Architect stations:

  • Launch: Select a launch vehicle class (compact rideshare, dedicated medium launcher, or heavy-lift reserve) matched to the spacecraft's total mass and mission cost constraints.
  • Power: Balance continuous spacecraft bus loads and peak instrument power demands using fixed solar arrays, sun-tracking arrays, or solar-plus-battery storage architectures, accounting for long shadow periods.
  • Science Instruments: Assemble a payload suite by weighing potential scientific return against dry mass, electrical power draw, onboard data generation rates, and procurement budget.
  • Communications: Configure the telecommunications architecture—choosing between low-gain, high-gain, or relay-assisted links—and evaluate how each option's downlink capacity constrains the volume of science data returned to Earth.
  • Operations: Define the operational concept, ranging from a short polar sortie to a precision landing or an extended surface survey, observing how mission duration influences total science yield, operational risk, budget, mass, power margins, and propellant reserves.
  • Trajectory: Evaluate orbital transfer and descent profiles, balancing propellant consumption, transit duration, and entry/descent risk against mission constraints.

Once the design is finalized, players execute their mission in a bundled 3D Flight Simulator that visualizes ascent,cislunar transfer, and approach to their chosen lunar landing site, accompanied by a live status board tracking resource margins in real time. Following the flight, a comprehensive evaluation and diagnostic report presents performance scores,subsystem diagnostics, and resource utilization breakdowns so learners can diagnose bottlenecks and iterate on their design. Every station also features an accessible, in-page field guide explaining foundational aerospace terms and engineering rules of thumb. NOVA functions strictly as an educational model for systems thinking rather than a certified flight-engineering or mission-prediction tool.

NASA Resources and Dynamic Scenario Generation

NOVA integrates authentic NASA datasets as scientific and educational reference context to ground its lunar visualization and learning modules. These resources include a NASA 3D lunar globe model, 2K surface imagery from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC), topographic reference context from the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA),and established NASA systems-engineering and mission-design frameworks.

To ensure high replayability and prevent rote memorization, NOVA features a seeded procedural scenario generator.Based on the player's chosen mission profile and target site, the engine generates tailored mission constraints and introduces controlled variables—such as tighter mass or budget caps, power drops, communications disruptions, data volume limits, schedule shifts, or propellant margin adjustments. Before any scenario logic is deployed, an automated verification test suite runs 1,000 generated scenarios per mission path to confirm that each has at least one viable solution.While NASA datasets anchor NOVA's visual environment and educational context, the randomized scenario parameters and calculated performance metrics belong to NOVA's simplified educational model and do not represent real-world NASA specifications or flight predictions.

Development, Tools, and Creativity

Engineered natively for the modern web using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Three.js, NOVA runs directly in a WebGL-enabled browser without requiring installation or plugins. Building the platform involved solving several key technical and design challenges: integrating NASA's 3D lunar globe and 2K LROC surface imagery into a lightweight, responsive Three.js scene; architecting a deterministic subsystem dependency engine that recalculates mass, power, data, propellant,and budget instantaneously after every user input; and pairing seeded procedural scenario generation with clear, intuitive visual diagnostics. Throughout the entire user journey, NOVA maintains clear transparency by distinguishing authentic NASA reference data from the simplified game mechanics designed for learning.
